title: What Extbase Is For, and When It Is Not Needed
hints: Extbase is what a frontend needs beyond reading records: pagination, a search with arguments, validation, forms. Rendering records read-only needs none of it — see the records hint — and mixing the two questions is where most of the wrong answers here come from.

The rest is its own hint: extbase-plugin-registration for the two calls that declare a plugin, extbase-domain-mapping for models and repositories, extbase-arguments for what arrives from a request, extbase-pagination for paging a list.

title: The Two Calls That Register a Plugin
hints: A plugin is registered by two calls that do different things. ExtensionUtility::registerPlugin() belongs in Configuration/TCA/Overrides/tt_content.php and adds the item to the CType selector, optionally with a FlexForm; ExtensionUtility::configurePlugin() belongs in ext_localconf.php and declares which controller actions exist and which of them are not cacheable. Neither one replaces the other.

The plugin signature both calls derive — the extension name and the plugin name, lowercased and joined by an underscore — is four things at once: the value in the CType column, the TypoScript key below tt_content, the key the FlexForm is registered under, and the namespace the plugin's own arguments arrive in. Renaming a plugin renames all four, and existing content keeps the old value.

hints.text: configurePlugin() takes a plugin type as its last argument that has to be omitted or given as "CType": a plugin is a content type of its own and nothing else, and anything else throws.
configurePlugin() still takes "list_type" as its last argument and warns about it. New code omits the argument or passes "CType", because that is the shape that survives the next major.

hints: ExtensionUtility::PLUGIN_TYPE_CONTENT_ELEMENT is the constant whose value is "CType", so a call passing the constant is passing the accepted value. The exception message quotes the literal, which is what makes a call written with the constant read as a violation of it.

hints.text: ExtensionUtility::PLUGIN_TYPE_PLUGIN went with the plugin subtype it named, so a call still passing it fails on the undefined constant before configurePlugin() is entered rather than on the check inside it.

title: Models, Repositories and the Table Behind Them
hints: A model maps onto the table its class name implies. Configuration/Extbase/Persistence/Classes.php is where a table named differently is mapped, together with the per-property column names and the record type of a single-table inheritance.
Orderings are property names, not column names. Ordering by the order records have in the backend therefore needs a property for that field on the model, although it is not a domain concept.

title: What Arrives From a Request, and What Silently Does Not
appliesTo: It is not allowed to map property
argument is missing from the link
hints: A search form submitted by GET on a cacheable action answers with a page-not-found, and putting the action into the non-cacheable list does not fix it: the cache hash is validated by a middleware, long before Extbase knows which action was called. The plugin's arguments have to be excluded from the hash as well, in $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['FE']['cacheHash']['excludedParameters']. A name there carries an indicator: ^ matches the beginning of a parameter name, ~ any part of it, and no indicator at all is an exact match — the one entry that covers a whole plugin is the prefix form. The hidden fields a Fluid form adds need the same treatment.

An object argument maps nothing until its properties are allowed. A request that hands a controller an object other than a persisted entity fails with "It is not allowed to map property" until the matching initialize<Action>Action() calls allowProperties() on that argument's property mapping configuration. That is the secure default rather than a defect.

An object that is not persisted is dropped from a generated link without a word: the URI builder serialises an entity by its uid, and something built for the request has none — so the filter of a search is gone on page two while the link looks correct. Pass such state to a link as plain arguments.

A Fluid form field registers its name in the trusted properties, and a real request maps only what they hold. A name that ends in [] registers a list, so its indices may map; f:form.select with multiple registers it once per option. A name without [] registers a scalar: the property may map and no child of it may. So a type converter that builds children from a scalar source fails in a request with "It is not allowed to map property". A test that builds its own PropertyMappingConfiguration passes all the same, because it never reads the trusted properties.

title: Paginating a List
hints: Which paginator to use follows from what is being paginated: QueryResultPaginator for an Extbase query result, QueryBuilderPaginator for a Doctrine query builder, ArrayPaginator for an array that is already in memory. The last one paginates in PHP, so choosing it for a query means every record is fetched in order to show one page. SlidingWindowPagination on top of any of them produces the page numbers.

A paginator clamps a page number outside its range, so a page beyond the last one answers with the first page rather than with a not-found. Compare the current page against the number of pages in the controller and answer with the not-found response yourself, or the same list is served under an unbounded number of URLs.

A paginated plugin needs a route for the list as well as one for the paginated form. A single route with the page number defaulted only omits the variable when a link is built, and the literal part of the segment stays behind — a link to the first page then points at a path that ends in the prefix of a number that is not there. Routes are tried in the order they are declared, so the paginated one goes before a route whose slug would otherwise swallow it.

title: How a Query Becomes SQL, and How Extbase Writes a Row
hints: Typo3DbQueryParser turns a Query into a Doctrine QueryBuilder, one operator at a time. It is the layer that decides what a constraint means in SQL, and reading it is faster than reasoning about QueryInterface: the whole translation is one match on the operator constant.

equals($property, null) is supported and becomes `IS NULL`; so does the explicit OPERATOR_EQUAL_TO_NULL. lessThan, greaterThan and in() bind a typed parameter instead. contains() with null throws BadConstraintException, exception 1484828468, rather than matching anything.
`IS NULL` only finds rows the column is actually NULL in, which is where a datetime property parts company with its column — tca-datetime-storage is that half.

ColumnMap is what the parser and the mapper look a property up in: the column name, the relation type, the tables and match fields behind a relation, and dateTimeStorageFormat, which is the TCA dbType carried onto the Extbase side by ColumnMapFactory. A property whose mapping is wrong fails here rather than in the SQL.

Extbase writes through Typo3DbBackend, which calls ConnectionPool directly — Backend::insertObject() and updateObject() build a row and hand it to addRow() or updateRow(). Nothing goes through DataHandler, so there is no hook, no history entry, no reference index update and no versioning. A test that expects any of those has to write through DataHandler instead.

insertObject() puts a property into the row only where its value is not null, so a null property is left out of the INSERT and the column default decides what is stored. That is a different outcome from writing NULL, and it is invisible in the object afterwards.
